problem_framing.rationale: The deck restates the decision exactly as posed (enter or not, and by which route) and turns all five board items (ambition, cap, payback, margin floor, bandwidth) into an explicit test grid on slide 5 for A, A at 32% ACoS, B and J. It names early what the answer turns on: ad cost for A, awareness-driven sell-through for B, and the conflict between the $40M ambition and the constraints. It also flags its reading of the ambiguous 'on the way to $40M' wording and asks the board to confirm it. Nothing material is missing.

storyline_coherence.rationale: The governing thought answers the question, the executive summary points map onto the sections, and almost every title is a claim its slide supports; the titles alone give the argument. Two flaws keep it from a 5. First, slide 5 says A is the only route 'within the limits' and the summary says A 'passes every financial test', yet the deck's own recommended planning basis (30–32% ACoS) fails the payback test. Second, there is redundancy: the recommendation and decisions are restated on slides 2, 13, 14 and 15, and slides 5 and 6 overlap. The slide 3 title also overstates Amazon's 41% share as 'most'.

evidence_and_reasoning.rationale: I re-derived the model and found every figure correct. Unit contributions are $10.73 and $7.55; A's cumulative cash is +2.4, +0.4 and −2.3 at 25%, 28% and 32% ACoS; break-even ACoS is 28.6% (27.0% at −10% volume); B peaks at $20.8M with a 4.5% group margin in 2027; B without the halo peaks at $24.3M; J reaches +$1.8M; CAGR is 17% and share 14.7%. Derivations are transparent, all critical evidence is used, including evidence against A (32% benchmark, two stalled Amazon-first brands, slowing pilot growth), and the correlation memo is handled correctly. It is not a 5 because of a few overstated claims. The '$40M in 2031–32' path extrapolates a flat 29% growth rate when plan growth is decelerating (87%, 52%, 29%), and this feeds a board decision item even though it is labelled illustrative. '41% = most' and the Saebom sequencing ('after reaching $30M on Amazon') go beyond the pack. B is not costed at the 2.6 median, and J has no sensitivity despite the claim that it pays back in every case.

strategic_judgment.rationale: The recommendation is clear and defensible (the key's R1): Amazon-led with gates, a retail gate raised to 20% with a door test, a $4M envelope, a stop trigger, an explicit reset of the $40M ambition, and stated conditions for bringing retail forward, slowing down, or preferring Japan. Alternatives are compared on the board's own criteria and no trap is fallen into. The material flaw is in the payback logic. The deck tells the board to plan on 30–32% ACoS, a basis on which A misses the four-year payback, but never squarely asks the board to accept or relax that constraint. The stop trigger (above 32% for two quarters) and the end-2027 gate (≤30%) are both looser than the 28.6% break-even, so A can fail payback without any trigger firing. Japan, the only option passing every hard constraint, is set aside as 'off-strategy' with limited weighing.

clarity_and_concision.rationale: The answer is in the title of slide 2 and the language is plain and precise, with numbers attached to every claim. At 15 body slides plus two appendices and about 4,000 words, it is somewhat longer than the decision needs. The recommendation is restated four times (slides 2, 13, 14, 15) and the cash and constraint slides overlap. This is strong but not minimal.

unsupported_claims.quote: Amazon is where most of it is bought
unsupported_claims.why: Table 2 gives Amazon 41% of K-beauty skincare sales: the largest channel, but not a majority.

unsupported_claims.quote: Saebom added 300 doors in 2025, after reaching about $30M on Amazon
unsupported_claims.why: The pack gives about $30M of total US revenue in 2025, the same year the doors were added. It does not say the $30M was all Amazon or that it came before the doors.

unsupported_claims.quote: J is the only option that pays back in every case we can model.
unsupported_claims.why: Only the single planning case for J was modelled; no downside sensitivity was run on J, so 'every case' overstates the evidence.

logical_contradictions.quote_a: Amazon-led is the only route that builds a US business within the limits
logical_contradictions.quote_b: Plan on 30–32% ACoS, not 25% ... ACoS 32% (scale benchmark): −2.3
logical_contradictions.why: On the ad-cost basis the deck itself tells the board to plan on, Option A misses the board's payback-by-2030 limit, so it is not 'within the limits' on the deck's own realistic case. The deck discloses the payback risk but still labels A as passing and does not ask the board to relax the constraint.

recommendation.summary: Enter the US in 2027 via Amazon (Option A) and decline the 600-door retail launch. Plan on 30–32% ACoS with a $4M peak-cash envelope and target ACoS of 28% or less. Fix labels and take listings in-house. Add retail only after Amazon sales pass $10M, aided awareness reaches 20% and a door test covers its own fixed costs. Reset the ambition to $25–30M in 2030 with $40M in 2031–32, and defer the Japan scale-up.
recommendation.rationale: The recommendation meets all four defensibility criteria. It compares options on the cap, payback and margin floor; it tests the 25% ACoS, 4.5 units/door/week and 1.3× halo assumptions against the pack's benchmarks; it states the payback break-even (28.6% ACoS) and gives checkpoints, a stop trigger and conditions that would change the view; and it says plainly that $40M by 2030 is not reachable within the constraints. Its weakness is that the gates (≤30% at end-2027, stop above 32%) are looser than the payback break-even, and it does not explicitly ask the board to accept a payback miss on its own planning basis.

hypothesis_handling.rationale: The deck keeps the CEO's Amazon-first route but changes four things: the ACoS basis moves from 25% to 30–32%, a $4M envelope is added, the retail awareness gate rises from 15% to 20% (because the 10–20% band median of 3.5 is below the 4.0 delisting line), and a door test replaces a national rollout. It surfaces the contradictions between plan and benchmark ACoS, between the retailer's 4.5 and the 2.6 median, and between the ambition and the constraints. It rejects the causal reading of the 0.71 correlation and treats the four-brand competitor set as direction, not proof. One soft spot: it proposes using the four new SKUs to lift repeat, although the pack says it is unclear whether repeat rises with more SKUs; this is framed as an action with a checkpoint, not asserted as fact.

output.overall_comment: This is a very strong document. Every calculation I re-derived matches the pack and the key: unit economics, A and B cash paths, group margin, break-even ACoS, tariff and volume sensitivities, the no-halo case and Japan. It uses the board's constraints as the decision grid, tests each planning assumption against the benchmarks, avoids all seven traps, and adds a useful insight beyond the key (the CEO's 15% awareness gate is too low because the 10–20% band median is below the delisting line). The main weakness is an unresolved tension: it tells the board to plan on 30–32% ACoS, a basis on which A fails the four-year payback, while still calling A 'within the limits' and setting stop triggers looser than the 28.6% break-even. Lesser issues are the constant-29% extrapolation behind the '$40M in 2031–32' decision item, a few overstated phrases ('most' for 41%, the Saebom sequencing), and repetition of the recommendation across four slides. Weighted score is about 4.15.
